KEY MESSAGE 1: Periods of showers/scattered thunderstorms 
through Saturday will bring localized flash flooding risk across
central Pennsylvania. Strong-to-severe storms also possible 
this afternoon/evening.

Weak llvl boundaries and areas of signif differential heating
gradient and topographic effects will be the weather influencers
for the midday through early evening hours today. Larger scale
forcing associated with the favorable right entrance region of 
a 50-60 kt upper level jet core will move gradually east across
the CWA this afternoon and evening and help to realize the 
hefty 2000-3500 j/kg CAPE in the form of localized strong 
pulse/multicell TSRA updrafts. Bands of significantly lower 1-6
hour Flash Flood Guidance values across portions of the Susq
Valley and Scent Mtns will have to be monitored closely this
afternoon as convection ramps up/moves east and feeds off the 
best instability across this same area. 

Weakening convection across the NW third of the CWA and extensive
cloud cover was leading to a notable min in instability with SB
CAPE of 500-1000 J/KG, similar to the setup we saw Thursday
afternoon/evening.

Previous... 


Activity on Thursday was largely driven by the terrain in
combination with a very moist airmass. Overall a similar
situation today and Saturday. Location of the more active
weather on Saturday may be a bit further to the east and south. 
That is still a ways out.

For the overnight hours into Friday morning, the main concern
aside from an isolated shower will be the potential for fog/low
stratus development with mainly clear skies and calm winds.

More information below. 

This concern will be highest in areas that received heavy 
rainfall across southern Pennsylvania on Thursday. Updated fog 
forecast does outline this potential with valley fog expected 
across the northern half of central Pennsylvania. Any fog 
formation likely mixes out quickly after sunrise and is out by 
9AM EDT.

First glance at the first couple of hours of 00Z 8/7 HREF 
ensemble guidance outlines an uptick in shower activity across
northern Ohio overnight compared to previous runs. Thus, have
increased PoPs slightly earlier across NW PA closer to sunrise
compared to previous forecast. Increasing humidity throughout
the day with ample instability (~1000-2000 J/kg across N/W PA 
and 2000+ J/kg across S/E PA) will likely allow for slightly 
more widespread coverage with more height falls observed in 
recent model guidance compared to this afternoon and evening. 
In terms of a severe threat, expect scattered thunderstorms to 
develop with potentially a slight uptick in coverage compared to
this afternoon. Isolated instances of strong-to-damaging winds 
appear to be the main hazard with these, mainly in the form of 
wet microbursts given the instability, moisture, and lift 
(trough approaching the area) in play.

The overly moist air mass, with PWATs exceeding the 90th
percentile across all of central Pennsylvania, will brings
another round of flash flooding concerns on Friday and Saturday,
mainly during the afternoon/evening hours. This flooding threat
could be minimized by more progressive storm motions; however,
given the amount of moisture, any shower/storm will likely bring
efficient rainfall to the region and any location (especially 
urban and poor drainage locations) that receive multiple rounds 
of heavy rainfall could experience localized flash flooding. 
Recent HREF PMMs does paint a corridor 2-3" rainfall amounts 
along the Pennsylvania Turnpike Friday afternoon/evening, which 
tracks with the ample moisture available. Do want to highlight 
that while this signal exists, location of this corridor remains
the main point of uncertainty at this time so remain weather 
aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings tomorrow 
afternoon/evening. Heavy rain signal on Saturday is more muted; 
however, if this heavier corridor of rain plays out as 
predicted, some locations could need very little rainfall for 
additional flooding concerns on Saturday.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Very warm temperatures and humid conditions will
lead to heat index values approaching 100 degrees across 
portions of the Lower Susquehanna Valley today.

Current grids only show a few grid points getting close. 
Also temperatures being push back down by showers and 
storms, temperatures may not stay up in that range for
very long anyway. 

More information below.

Increasing heat and humidity throughout the afternoon hours 
ahead of the aforementioned showers/storms will lead to another 
hot day across portions of the Lower Susquehanna Valley and 
surrounding locations. Recent model guidance does indicate a 
slight decrease in temperatures tomorrow with increasing cloud 
cover during the late morning/early afternoon hours across the 
region which could limit peak heating slightly. That being said,
